Mukkuri的聆聽示範主要見於阿伊努傳統音樂錄音，常與撥弦樂器 tonkori: Listening examples for the mukkuri come mostly from recordings of Ainu traditional music, often in ensemble with the plucked string instrument tonkori. Since the 1960s recordings of Ainu traditional music have carried the mukkuri's sound less often; Umeko Andō's album 《安東ウメ子・ムックリの世界》 presents her playing directly, and Akira Ifukube's biographical television drama 《北の交響曲》 also invited Andō to play. Shigiko Teshi's Homage to the Rivers of the World is another recording of Ainu music.

Mukkuri（暫譯）是日本阿伊努民族的傳統撥奏體鳴樂器，屬口弦一類，非沙鈴或刮: The mukkuri (provisional name) is a traditional plucked idiophone of the Ainu of Japan, a kind of Jew's harp rather than a shaker or scraper. It is made of bamboo and measures 10 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. The player holds the lamella at the mouth and pulls a string to set the lamella vibrating. It is common in Ainu traditional music and is often played in ensemble with the plucked string instrument tonkori; the source also mentions its use in documentaries, music recordings, competitions, television drama and museum workshops.
來源明確記載 mukkuri 為日本阿伊努民族傳統撥奏體鳴樂器，琴身以竹製成。發: The source states clearly that the mukkuri is a traditional plucked idiophone of the Ainu of Japan and that its frame is made of bamboo. To sound it the player pulls a string so that the lamella vibrates, holding the lamella at the mouth. The source does not say whether the lamella is also bamboo, nor the material of the string or of the other parts of the frame, so bamboo is the only material that can be confirmed.

暮樂的音色具有獨特的溫潤與穿透力並存的特質。其聲音明亮卻帶有暗沉的底蘊，散發出原: The mukkuri's timbre is at once warm and penetrating. Its sound is bright yet has a dark undertone, and gives off a raw, mysterious air. Its range sits in the upper middle frequencies, and its volume is relatively small yet highly expressive. In playing, the mouth acts as the resonating cavity: shifting the position of the tongue and the shape of the lips yields a wide range of timbral change, which lends the sound a trance-like quality. Compared with the crisp sharpness of the Jew's harp, the mukkuri sounds gentler and softer; compared with the harmonica, its timbre has more of an Eastern character and more of a national flavour. The sound of this raw yet finely made instrument often carries subtle partials and overtones, conjuring musical images that seem to come from the distant past.
暮樂（Mukkuri）是日本北海道阿伊努民族的傳統樂器，距今已有數百年歷史。該樂: The mukkuri is a traditional instrument of the Ainu of Hokkaido in Japan, several hundred years old. It dates from the period of Ainu hunting culture and was originally made of bamboo; it is an important musical tool in the daily life and rituals of the people. The player holds the instrument at the mouth and pulls a string to set the lamella vibrating. Its distinctive timbre is deeply woven into Ainu musical tradition.

隨著時間推移，暮樂逐漸成為阿伊努文化的象徵樂器。在日本文化交流中，這種樂器從北海: Over time the mukkuri became a symbolic instrument of Ainu culture. Through cultural exchange within Japan the instrument came to be known from Hokkaido gradually to wider Japanese society. In modern times it has been valued and protected as intangible cultural heritage, and many musicians work to pass on and improve the craft. Today the mukkuri has gone beyond its region and holds a place in international folk-music exchange, as an important medium for introducing Ainu culture.
